## Introduction

Let $X$ be a [[random-variables|random variable]] with density $f_{X}$ (or mass
function) and let $g:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a measurable function. This
note covers methods for finding the properties of the new random variable
$Y=g(X)$: its expectation, moments and distribution.

## Fundamental theorem

:::{.theorem data-title="Fundamental theorem"}

Let $X$ have density $f_{X}$ and let $g:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be measurable
with $g(X)$ integrable. Then $Y=g(X)$ has expectation
$$
\mathbb{E}[Y]=\int_{\Omega}g(X)\,d\mathbb{P}=\int_{\mathbb{R}}g(x)f_{X}(x)\,dx.
$$

:::

In the discrete case the integral becomes a sum over the support of $X$ with
mass function $p_{X}(x)$.

In general $\mathbb{E}[g(X)]\neq g(\mathbb{E}[X])$. Equality is guaranteed
for every distribution only when $g$ is an [[affine-function]], that is, a
linear function plus a translation (for convex $g$ see
[[jensen-inequality]]).

## Distribution of the transformed variable

Recall that the **inverse image** (preimage) of a set $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$
under $g$ is
$$
g^{-1}(A):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}:g(x)\in A\},
$$
see [[images-and-preimages]]. It satisfies $g^{-1}(\mathbb{R})=\mathbb{R}$,
$g^{-1}(A^c)=g^{-1}(A)^c$ and
$g^{-1}(\bigcup_\lambda A_\lambda)=\bigcup_\lambda g^{-1}(A_\lambda)$. As a
result, $\mu(A)=\mathbb{P}(X\in g^{-1}(A))=\mathbb{P}(g(X)\in A)$ satisfies the
axioms of probability and is the **distribution** of $Y=g(X)$ (see
[[random-variables]] and [[probability-spaces]]).

### Discrete transformations

If $X$ is discrete with mass function $f_{X}$, then $Y=g(X)$ has mass
function
$$
f_{Y}(y)=\sum_{x\in g^{-1}(\{y\})}f_{X}(x).
$$

:::{.example}

Let $X\sim\mathcal{P}(\lambda)$ follow a [[poisson-distribution]] and define
$Y=g(X)=X^2+7$. The support of $X$ is $\mathbb{N}_{0}$, on which $g$ is
one-to-one, so
$$
f_{Y}(y)=f_{X}\big(\sqrt{y-7}\big)
=\frac{\lambda^{\sqrt{y-7}}e^{-\lambda}}{\big(\sqrt{y-7}\big)!},
$$
on the support $y\in\{x^2+7:x\in\mathbb{N}_0\}=\{7,8,11,16,\dots\}$.

:::

### Continuous transformations

Suppose $g$ is **one-to-one**, that is strictly increasing or strictly
decreasing (hence $g^{-1}$ is too). The **CDF method** computes, in the
increasing case,
$$
\mathbb{P}(Y\leq y)=\mathbb{P}(g(X)\leq y)=\mathbb{P}(X\leq g^{-1}(y))
=F_{X}(g^{-1}(y)),
$$
and in the decreasing case $1-F_{X}(g^{-1}(y))$ (for continuous $X$).
Differentiating by the chain rule, and taking the modulus to cover both cases,
$$
f_{Y}(y)=f_{X}(g^{-1}(y))\left|\frac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y)\right|.
$$

Special care is needed when $g$ is not one-to-one, for example $g(x)=x^2$ or
$g(x)=|x|$ on $\mathbb{R}$. For $g(x)=x^2$ and $y>0$,
$$
F_{Y}(y)=\mathbb{P}(X^2\leq y)=\mathbb{P}(-\sqrt{y}\leq X\leq\sqrt{y})
=F_{X}(\sqrt{y})-F_{X}(-\sqrt{y}),
$$
and differentiating gives
$$
f_{Y}(y)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\Big\{f_{X}(\sqrt{y})+f_{X}(-\sqrt{y})\Big\}.
$$
If $f_{X}$ is symmetric about the origin this simplifies to
$f_{Y}(y)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}f_{X}(\sqrt{y})$.

:::{.example}

Let $Z$ follow the standard [[normal-distribution]] with density
$\phi(z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z^2/2}$. The density is symmetric, so
$Y=Z^2$ has density
$$
f_{Y}(y)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}\phi(\sqrt{y})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi y}}e^{-y/2},
\qquad y>0,
$$
which is the [[chi-squared-distribution]] with one degree of freedom.

:::

## The probability integral transform

:::{.proposition data-title="Probability integral transform"}

Let $X$ be a continuous random variable whose distribution function $F_{X}$
is strictly increasing on the support of $X$ (so $F_X$ is invertible). Then
$U=F_{X}(X)$ is uniform on $[0,1]$.

:::

:::{.proof}

For $u\in[0,1]$,
$$
\mathbb{P}(U\leq u)=\mathbb{P}(F_{X}(X)\leq u)=\mathbb{P}(X\leq F_{X}^{-1}(u))
=F_{X}(F_{X}^{-1}(u))=u.
$$

:::

So $U$ follows the [[continuous-uniform-distribution]] on $[0,1]$. Most
random number generators simulate independent copies of $U$. Conversely, we
can simulate a random variable with distribution function $F_{X}$ by drawing
$U$ and setting
$$
X=F_{X}^{-1}(U).
$$
This is **inverse transform sampling**.
